findings.summary: The handbook stops after 3xx — the 4xx, 5xx, and decision-rule chapters are missing entirely, so earlier pages and the caption reference codes that are never defined.
findings.evidence: Content has 9 slides ending at "3xx: Permanence and Method Rewriting", yet the caption promises "Ten pages of dense notes" and "the exact difference between 401 and 403, 400 and 422, 502 and 504" — 401, 403, 400, 422, 502, 504 appear nowhere in the slides. Page 5 says "Stale etag returns 412 Precondition Failed" and page 6 tabulates "409 Conflict", "403 Forbidden", "405 Method Not Allowed" with no page ever explaining them.
findings.fix: Add the three missing chapters as pages 10–12 (4xx Client Errors, 5xx Server Errors & Retries, Choosing the Right Code) before publication; if the part is intentionally split, cut the caption's "ten pages" and its 401/403, 400/422, 502/504 promises and mark it Part 1 of 2.

findings.summary: The caption promises page count and 4xx/5xx comparisons that the deck does not contain.
findings.evidence: Caption: "the exact difference between 401 and 403, 400 and 422, 502 and 504. Ten pages of dense notes" — the set has 9 pages and stops at 3xx; 401, 403, 400, 422, 502 and 504 appear nowhere in the slides.
findings.fix: Either add the 4xx/5xx pages the caption advertises, or rewrite the caption to match the delivered scope (methods, 1xx–3xx) and the actual nine-page count.

findings.summary: The caption promises 4xx and 5xx coverage that no page in the deck delivers, since the titles stop at 3xx.
findings.evidence: Caption: "the exact difference between 401 and 403, 400 and 422, 502 and 504" — but the last title is "3xx: Permanence and Method Rewriting", with no 4xx or 5xx page in the list.
findings.fix: Either rewrite the caption's specifics to name examples the deck actually covers (e.g. "why 302 after a POST eats your form body, and what safe/idempotent/cacheable really mean across GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE"), or add the missing 4xx and 5xx pages before publishing.

findings.summary: JSON Merge Patch is cited as RFC 7386, which was obsoleted by RFC 7396 in the same month it was published.
findings.evidence: "JSON Patch RFC 6902, JSON Merge Patch RFC 7386" — RFC 7386 (Oct 2014) is marked Obsoleted by RFC 7396; page 5 of this same set correctly uses the RFC 7396 media type `application/merge-patch+json`.
findings.fix: Change to "JSON Merge Patch RFC 7396" (optionally noting it obsoletes the short-lived RFC 7386).

findings.summary: The section heading calls safe, idempotent, and cacheable "independent axes" while the callout two blocks later states that safe implies idempotent, contradicting it.
findings.evidence: Heading: "Three Independent Axes" — followed on the same page by callout "Safe Implies Idempotent": "The reverse is false: PUT and DELETE change state, but repeating them changes nothing further."
findings.fix: Retitle the heading to "Three Properties" (or "Safe, Idempotent, Cacheable") so it does not assert independence the page immediately refutes.

findings.summary: Page titles are offset one page behind their content, so each chapter's definitions land under the previous chapter's title.
findings.evidence: The entire definitional core of safe/idempotent/cacheable ("Three Independent Axes", "Idempotence", "Cacheability", the safe/idem/cache table) sits on page 2, titled "Anatomy of a Method (cont.)", while page 3, titled "Safe, Idempotent, Cacheable", opens mid-topic at "PATCH Is The Odd One" and ends with GET-depth material ("Bodies and URL Limits", "Conditional and Range"). The same offset repeats: page 4 "GET, HEAD and OPTIONS in Depth" ends with "Who Names The URL", and page 7 "DELETE... (cont.)" carries "Reading A Status Line" and the 1xx codes.
findings.fix: Repaginate so each chapter's first block starts on the page bearing its title — move the "Three Independent Axes" block onward to page 3, "Bodies and URL Limits" onward to page 4, "Who Names The URL" to page 5, and "Reading A Status Line" onward to page 8 — adding "(cont.)" pages where a chapter genuinely overflows.

findings.summary: "An absolute merge patch is idempotent" is asserted with no example, and merge-patch syntax is not shown until page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 3 bullets: "An append op grows the array on every call" / "An absolute merge patch is idempotent" — the adjacent code block only shows the JSON Patch case `{"op":"add","path":"/tags/-","value":"x"}`. The first merge-patch document, `{"email": null}`, appears on page 5.
findings.fix: Add the contrasting example to the page-3 code block, e.g. `{"status":"paid"}  // merge patch: same result every time`, so both halves of the PATCH idempotence claim are shown.

findings.summary: 201 Created is described as requiring a Location header, but RFC 9110 makes Location optional.
findings.evidence: "201 Created: a new resource exists, MUST include `Location:`" vs RFC 9110 §15.3.2: "The primary resource created by the request is identified by either a Location header field in the response or, if no Location header field is received, by the target URI."
findings.fix: Reword to "201 Created: a new resource exists; send `Location:` unless the created resource is the request URI (e.g. a PUT create)".

findings.summary: The 303/307 split is attributed to RFC 7231 (2014) when those codes were introduced by HTTP/1.1 in 1997.
findings.evidence: "RFC 7231 split the semantics into 303 and 307" — 303 See Other and 307 Temporary Redirect were added in RFC 2068 (HTTP/1.1, 1997) and carried into RFC 2616 (1999); RFC 7231 only revised them, and the current spec is RFC 9110.
findings.fix: Change to "HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2068/2616) added 303 and 307 to make the intent unambiguous; RFC 9110 is the current definition".

findings.summary: The redirect cheat-sheet table on page 8 prescribes 303, 307, and 308 before page 9 defines what any of them do.
findings.evidence: Page 8 ends with "RFC 7231 split the semantics into 303 and 307" and the table rows "temporary + preserve | 307" and "permanent + preserve | 308"; the definitions arrive only on page 9: "303 See Other always switches the client to GET", "307 Temporary Redirect MUST preserve method and body", "308 is 301 that preserves method and body".
findings.fix: Move the "Permanent vs Temporary" heading, the 302-problem bullets, and the cheat-sheet table from page 8 to page 9, placing the table after the "Method Rewriting" block so every code in it has already been defined.

findings.summary: The caption states a page count that does not match the number of pages in the carousel.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ten pages of dense notes"; the titles array contains nine entries, ending at "3xx: Permanence and Method Rewriting".
findings.fix: Change "Ten pages" to "Nine pages", or restore the tenth page if one was dropped.

findings.summary: Case-sensitivity of methods is turned into a MUST-reject rule that no RFC states.
findings.evidence: "`get` is not `GET` — servers must reject it" — RFC 9110 §9.1 makes the method token case-sensitive and says an origin server that receives an unrecognized or unimplemented method SHOULD respond with 501 Not Implemented.
findings.fix: Reword to "`get` is not `GET` — an unrecognized method gets 501 Not Implemented, never silent normalization".

findings.summary: ETags are used as the validator for conditional requests and optimistic locking but are never defined anywhere in the handbook.
findings.evidence: Page 3 shows `If-None-Match: "a1b2"   -> 304, no body` with no prior mention of what an entity tag is; page 5 then relies on it ("Guard PUT/PATCH with `If-Match: \"etag\"`", "Stale etag returns 412") and page 9 only says "MUST include the validators such as `ETag`".
findings.fix: Add one bullet before the "Conditional and Range" code block on page 3: "`ETag: \"a1b2\"` — an opaque server-issued version tag for a representation; clients echo it in `If-None-Match`/`If-Match`."

findings.summary: Two HEAD rules are overstated: identical headers are a SHOULD, and `Content-Length: 0` is legitimate for an empty resource.
findings.evidence: "Must return exactly the headers GET would" and "A server sending `Content-Length: 0` on HEAD is broken" — RFC 9110 §9.3.2 says a server SHOULD send the same header fields as for GET but MAY omit fields "for which a value is determined only while generating the content".
findings.fix: Reword to "Should send the same headers GET would; a server MAY omit fields it can only compute by generating the body" and "`Content-Length: 0` on HEAD is a bug unless the GET body really would be empty".

findings.summary: The reason-phrase rule is stated as MUST when the spec says SHOULD.
findings.evidence: "# clients MUST ignore the phrase" vs RFC 9112 §4: "A client SHOULD ignore the reason-phrase content because it is not a reliable channel for information".
findings.fix: Change the comment to "# clients SHOULD ignore the phrase".

findings.summary: The page title names two sections that live on the previous page while half this page is 3xx material.
findings.evidence: Page 8 is titled "Status Anatomy, 1xx and 2xx", but the status-line anatomy ("# 3 digits + reason phrase") and the whole 1xx section (100/101/103) are on page 7; page 8 instead ends with "301 Moved Permanently", "302 Found" and the permanent-vs-temporary table.
findings.fix: Retitle page 7 to cover status anatomy and 1xx, and page 8 to "2xx and the Redirect Families" (or move the 301/302 blocks onto page 9) so each title matches its own page.

findings.summary: 303 is said to always switch the client to GET, but a redirected HEAD stays HEAD.
findings.evidence: "303 See Other always switches the client to GET" — RFC 9110 §15.4.4 lets the user agent "perform a retrieval request targeting that URI (a GET or HEAD request if using HTTP)".
findings.fix: Reword to "303 See Other switches the client to a retrieval request — GET (or HEAD if the original was HEAD)".
